items.title: Georg Brunis Interview, 1958-06-03
items.q: Well, you see Teagarden plays nothing but soft solos.

ctx.x: Do you think you're apt to ruin your lip by trying to play too high, or what would you?

Well, you see Teagarden plays nothing but soft solos. And he don't, he don't enforce himself on ensemble. Sometimes you don't know Jack's in the band when they play an ensemble. That's right. Because he saves that lip. His lip is flexible for those pretty little uh, lip trails, the thing he does on the solos. It's what you call a specialist. But if he blasts like I did, he couldn't play them soft solos like he does. He doesn't have. He doesn't have to play one way or the other. Me, I smear into it and I jump up…

Yeah. You might use a lot of variety, but you, in the old days, that's what I wonder. I never heard you see 30 years ago. Uh, now you play something so soft and sweet and all to you and then you get the same music.

items.title: Jack Teagarden Interview, 1959-10-29
items.q: It was Paul Marys and George Brunas, and they were up there.

ctx.x: Who was around New Orleans there?

Well, uh, Harry Shields was here. The Dixieland Band was gone. New Orleans Rhythm Kings were in Chicago. It was Paul Marys and George Brunas, and they were up there. I think there was a, most everybody was kind of out of town at that time. At least when I came over here, there wasn't very much doing.
Who was in the band with Wingy that you worked with?
